title: Food & drink
goal: Order food and drinks, say what you want and don't want, and say what you like.
intro:
Kerala food is built around **rice** (ചോറ് *chōṟŭ*), coconut, fish and spices; breakfast staples include **puttu**, **appam** and **dosa**. 'Have you eaten?' (ഭക്ഷണം കഴിച്ചോ? / ചോറുണ്ടോ?) is a standard friendly greeting.

Grammatically, this unit introduces a key Malayalam pattern: the **dative subject**. 'I want', 'I like', 'I'm hungry' are expressed as 'to me there is want / liking / hunger': എനിക്ക് വേണം, എനിക്ക് ഇഷ്ടമാണ്, എനിക്ക് വിശക്കുന്നു.

vocab.en: curry; any side dish with gravy

vocab.note: Often means beef in Kerala; also മാംസം (formal).
Kerala tea is milky and sweet; കട്ടൻ ചായ = black tea.

vocab.en: lunch; rice meal (served on a plate/leaf)
vocab.note: Restaurant boards say ഊണ് റെഡി 'meals ready'.
With dative: എനിക്ക് ... വേണം 'I want…'. Question: വേണോ?
Past: കഴിച്ചു. തിന്നുക 'to eat' is blunt/informal.

phrases.en: Two teas, please! (calling to the man at the stall)
Could you give me some water?
It's delicious! (lit. there is good taste)
Enough, I'm full. (lit. the stomach filled)

grammar.title: Wanting: എനിക്ക് ... വേണം / വേണ്ട
grammar.body:
'Want / need' is **വേണം** *vēṇam*, and 'don't want' is **വേണ്ട** *vēṇḍa*. The person who wants goes in the **dative** (-ക്ക് / -ന്): **എനിക്ക്** ചായ **വേണം** 'to me tea is wanted' = 'I want tea'. Like all Malayalam verbs, വേണം doesn't change for person.

To ask, add -ഓ: **വേണോ?** *vēṇō?* 'do you want (it)?'. In shops and cafés the subject is usually dropped: ചായ വേണോ? — വേണം / വേണ്ട. The thing wanted needs no special ending.

(വേണം also means 'must' with verbs — that comes in unit 15.)

grammar.title: Liking and feeling: the dative subject
grammar.body:
Many experiences in Malayalam are things that happen **to** you, so the experiencer takes the **dative**:

• **ഇഷ്ടം** 'liking': എനിക്ക് ചായ **ഇഷ്ടമാണ്** 'I like tea'; negative ഇഷ്ടമല്ല / ഇഷ്ടമില്ല.
• **വിശക്കുന്നു** 'is hungry', **ദാഹിക്കുന്നു** 'is thirsty': എനിക്ക് വിശക്കുന്നു.
• **അറിയാം** 'know' (unit 2), **മനസ്സിലായി** 'understood'.

Compare normal subjects with ordinary action verbs: **ഞാൻ** ചായ കുടിക്കുന്നു 'I drink tea'. Tastes are nouns used with ഉണ്ട്: എരിവ് ഉണ്ട് 'it's spicy' (lit. there is spiciness).

dialogue.title: At the tea shop
dialogue.setting: Ravi and his friend Lisa stop at a roadside ചായക്കട (tea shop) in the morning.

lines.speaker: Ravi
lines.native: ചേട്ടാ, രണ്ട് ചായ. ലിസയ്ക്ക് പഞ്ചസാര വേണോ?
lines.roman: chēṭṭā, raṇḍŭ chāya. Lisaykkŭ pañjasāra vēṇō?
lines.en: Two teas, please. Lisa, do you want sugar?

lines.speaker: Shopkeeper
lines.native: കഴിക്കാൻ എന്തെങ്കിലും വേണോ? പുട്ടും കടലയും ഉണ്ട്, അപ്പവും മുട്ടക്കറിയും ഉണ്ട്.
lines.roman: kaḻikkān endeṅgilum vēṇō? puṭṭum kaṭalayum uṇḍŭ, appavum muṭṭakkaṟiyum uṇḍŭ.
lines.en: Anything to eat? There's puttu and chickpea curry, and appam and egg curry.

lines.speaker: Lisa
lines.en: Appam and egg curry for me. Is it very spicy?

lines.speaker: Ravi
lines.en: Puttu and chickpea curry for me.

lines.speaker: Ravi
lines.en: Chettan, how much is the bill?

culture: A traditional സദ്യ (sadya, feast — e.g. at Onam or weddings) is served on a banana leaf and eaten with the right hand, with up to 20+ dishes. Hosts will keep refilling your plate; to stop, say മതി! (enough) and cover the leaf with your hand. Kerala has India's highest per-capita fish consumption, and many Malayalis — Hindu, Christian and Muslim — eat beef and fish.
